newsitem.title: GERMANY: German grain intervention seen starting slowly.
newsitem.headline: German grain intervention seen starting slowly.

text.p: Sales into German public grain stocks are expected to be small and slow in the next few weeks, a source at state grain intervention board BLE said on Friday.

"There is interest in rye and barley intervention in eastern Germany and in small volumes in northern Germany, but all in all we will see a sluggish start," he said on the first day of the November-May buying campaign..
"Free market prices are very high and will ease at some stage, but I don't want to participate in speculation over the timing and the likelihood of intervention purchases."
"It also hinges on the volumes and rebates allowed by the EU for third country exports."
Sellers were slow to emerge, with a religious holiday being observed in several states.
Sales offers were not expected to pick up next week, he added.
BLE purchases totalled 1.7 million tonnes in the 1995/96 campaign, when high world market prices made sales into state stores unattractive.
After a speedy start last November and December, sales came to a virtual standstill earlier this year.
"This time the pattern could be the other way around -- small volumes this year and perhaps larger quantities in 1997," the BLE source said.
Germany harvested a record crop of 42 million tonnes in 1996, up 5.3 percent.
The November buying-in price is 231.49 marks per tonne for all grains, well below free market prices.
Traders said only rye in some parts of eastern Germany was cheaper.
